en: The gateways of yoga all arise from contemplation upon the seed-syllables of the Sanskrit script, giving birth to all manner of vast and great spiritual transformations to universally benefit sentient beings. This root text first lists twenty syllables;

practitioners must ensure their visualization and recollection of these are thoroughly mastered before ascending the altar to perform the rites. The structure of these characters each possesses natural rules that allow no deviation.
There are discrepancies down to the finest detail. Examining the original edition from Bao Hua Temple, it was already not entirely consistent with the style and structure of the Indic texts;
subsequent re-engravings have only made the divergence even more remote. Now, following the Dragon Canon (Longzang), I have collated and verified this with all my heart. As for the first three lines:
This comprises fifteen characters in total, all of which have now been revised. Regarding the five characters in the final line, there remain points of uncertainty;
thus, I have appended a few words of inquiry. I humbly beseech the eminent scholars who have delved deeply into the ocean of the Dharma to further examine and correct this work.
This is what I deeply rejoice in; the pronunciation is *wa*. If the radical is added, it is pronounced *so*, *ye*, or *yan*.
Since the characters *yan* and *yan* have similar pronunciations, if the radical is added, it is also pronounced *yan*, *la*, or *la*.
Originally it was written with the pronunciation *lan*; upon examining the Tibetan script, it is mostly written as such, and its pronunciation is [as follows].
Regarding the character *lán* (藍): it is unknown upon what basis this is based. If the vowel *ra* is added, it is pronounced *lǎn*;

if the vowel *ha* is added, it is pronounced *hā*, or alternatively *hàn*. Furthermore, in the visualization section of the *Śrī-bali-vidhi*, there is the sound *dva-raṃ* (a conjunct syllable), which is precisely the addition of the vowel *ra*. Students should take note of this.
In the maṇḍala, the mudrā of the right hand indicates the pāramitās, and the mudrā of the left hand indicates the pāramitās;
these two hands together specifically demonstrate the ten pāramitās. Thus it is performed.
The self-hand visualization is clear in its sequence. Regarding the hand-mudrās in the concentration [section], all are performed as visualizations facing another person;
that which is on the left is placed on the right, and that which is on the right is placed on the left.

Students should know that there are many versions of the *Yogācārya-bhikṣu-saṃgraha-bali-vidhi* (The Ritual Manual for the Bestowal of Food according to the Essential Yoga) in the Tibetan Canon (*Bka’ ’gyur*). Among them, the very first consists solely of the dhāraṇī revealed by the Buddha to Ānanda.

It originally consisted of only one chapter, yet the instruction was that it be recited twenty-one times; this is precisely what the present *Bhaktābhivardhana-mantra* (Food Transformation Mantra) is.

Thereafter, it gradually expanded until it reached the work commonly known among the laity as the *Yogacaryābhūmi-saṃgraha*, which is both detailed and exhaustive, such that it could not be further increased.
Nevertheless, at certain times, masters further appended external collections, causing the text to proliferate and become a tangled mass.

Alas! We have gradually lost the ancient spirit. To cite the most egregious examples: the "Five Vaipulya Offerings. Now, *vaipulya* (布), *sūtra* (思), *pāramitā* (度), and *samatā* (等) are all already Sanskrit terms;
why then apply the term "Vaipulya" (*fan*) again to them? Likewise, regarding the "Thirty-five Seals" (*mudrā*), a seal must necessarily have something received [by it].

As for the "Fifty-three Buddhas," with one Buddha and one seal for each, I do not know from which sūtra they originated. Consequently, more than half of these [practices] have become mere empty light.
They intersperse their recitations with idle chatter, yet at the most essential passages, they pass by as swiftly as a flowing stream; is this not merely laborious toil without merit?
Moreover, as the woodblocks have long been blurred by age, the seed-syllables of the former Buddhas are so obscured that they can no longer be distinguished.

To abandon carving for transcription is further to have nearly eliminated the ancient sages’ commentaries and annotations. Furthermore, once these seed-syllables are extinguished, [the Dharma will perish].
When observing from what something arises, if one merely dismisses it, then although the observation remains, one knows not how to employ it.

Recently, there have been those who have arisen to correct this, yet they still occasionally lose the proper sequence of priority; the refined and the vulgar alike have not yet been fully rectified, and those with discernment find this a source of concern.

The lay practitioner Xinxian, Mr. Bao, has conceived a vast and noble resolve to assemble various carvers to engrave the entire Tripitaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, thereby supplementing what previous individuals had failed to achieve.

It is my hope that those who ascend the dharma-throne will understand that Yoga refers to the perfect correspondence of the three karmas.

This single incense offering does not descend from heaven, nor does it sprout from the earth; before the two polarities were yet divided, its root source...
It fills the three realms. From the moment the single breath was first divided, its branches and leaves have spread throughout the ten directions.

It surpasses the brilliance of the sun and moon and eclipses the exquisite beauty of mountains and rivers. It is simultaneously precept, concentration, and wisdom; it is neither wood, nor fire, nor smoke.
When gathered, it is contained within a single mote of dust; when dispersed, it universally perfumes the entire Dharma-realm. As it is burned within the incense burner, focus [your mind]...
I extend this offering to the eternally abiding Triple Gem; to the myriad spirits of the ocean of lands; to the ancestral masters of successive generations; to all the assembly of holy ones;

and to all classes of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whether hidden or manifest, saintly or ordinary—relying entirely upon this true incense, may they all be universally and equally honored.

With a sincere heart, we take refuge and pay homage to the Buddha, the Honored One Among the Two-Legged, whose three types of awakening are perfected and who is endowed with myriad virtues—the Teacher and Tamer of Gods and Humans (Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ).

He is the Great Compassionate Father of both the mundane and the sagely. From the realm of ultimate reality, he manifests in responsive form; his compassionate transformation is universal, establishing [the Dharma] throughout the vertical world.

Pervading the three periods of time and extending horizontally throughout the ten directions, he thunders the Dharma’s rain and beats the Dharma’s drum, extensively expounding the provisional and ultimate teachings (*oṃ āḥ hūṃ*).
He opens wide the path of skillful means; if one takes refuge, one can extinguish the sufferings of hell.

With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to the Dharma-jaya, the Honored One who has transcended desire. Gathered within a precious treasury and stored in a jade casket, it was compiled in the Western Regions (Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ).
Translated and transmitted to the Eastern Land, the Patriarchs propagated it and the sages adjudicated it, composing commentaries and sub-commentaries.

It distinguishes the three vehicles into sudden and gradual teachings, and establishes the essential purport of the five doctrines. Venerated by ghosts and spirits, protected by dragons and devas, it guides the deluded and points toward the moon.
[Pointing with] Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ. This true nectar removes heat. If one takes refuge, it can extinguish the suffering of the hungry ghosts (preta).
With a sincere heart, I take refuge in and pay homage to the Saṅgha: the Honored One among the assembly, the teacher of the five virtues, and the companion of the six harmonies.

returning to the state of correctness is the 'ultimate. This is also the non-duality of the beginning and the source. The Master said: "To release and not withdraw is like an ordinary person; to withdraw and not release is called a Śrāvaka; to both withdraw and release is named the secret realm.)

The total non-employment of gathering and releasing is called "non-conceptual proliferation" (*niṣprapañca*). This is the most ultimate *mūlatantra*. The single character "gathering" (收) has been circulated so easily and lightly that students must not regard it as a trivial matter of hearsay or superficial observation.
Furthermore, bind the seal of the Sovereign Avalokiteśvara,

empower the four locations, and recite the secret mantra (these two phrases both refer to the practitioner’s request for the hidden empowerment of the Wisdom Buddha; as for the "secret mantra," it refers to the secret mantra of the hand seal mentioned below).

"One observes oneself as equal to Avalokiteśvara" (The preceding section has already involved observing Avalokiteśvara; now, fearing that one might lose sight of oneself and pursue external objects, one turns back to observe one's own body, hence the word "also. Since at the outset one used the seed-syllable to develop and bring about the realization of Avalokiteśvara, why is it said here again that one is "equal to" him?)

The answer states: "At first, the increase occurred because one had not yet transcended conceptualization; now, it is direct realization and direct entry, such as when Sudhana first beheld Mañjuśrī and others. Furthermore, the Avalokiteśvara previously conceived through thought is called 'the fruit within the cause' from the perspective of the causal stage.
Following the empowerment of the secret mantra, the very essence itself is 'the cause within the fruit.'"

[Question: "When one first enters the maṇḍala, one immediately gives rise to the pride (*māna*) of Avalokiteśvara. Why does one enter this samādhi again now? Is this not a case of confusion? [Answer: "No. The former was the fundamental samādhi; it is also called the 'correct position' (*samyag-avasthā*) and the 'correct essence' (*samyak-svabhāva*)."

It is like being a person who is a layman [at home]. The meditative absorption entered thereafter is the "accomplished" (*kṛtya*) absorption, which is like being a minister serving in a state. In reality, they are of one essence, though distinguished by their respective locations. It is also like a person wearing court robes when at court and military attire when on campaign;

thus, while the fundamental absorption is white in color, the accomplished absorption is golden. As one proceeds downward through each successive ritual procedure, there are many changes in the color of the body. One should discern this according to this principle.
By means of the supreme merit of this meditative concentration,
may it be dedicated so that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm may together behold the Western Land of Immeasurable Light.
To accomplish the vast vows of Samantabhadra (form the seal of the Sovereign Avalokiteśvara:

cross the two hands with the palms facing outward; join the tips of the index fingers like lotus petals; stand the two thumbs side by side. While reciting the mantra, empower the four places: the crown of the head, the throat, the heart, and the navel).
Oṃ vajratālamahriḥ. (The mudrā and mantra may be understood as before.
At each location, press with the hand-mudrā and recite the mantra once.)
Next, further empower with the syllable Oṃ and place the mudrā upon the mouth. Then,
empower the crown of the head with the syllable Hūṃ.
The syllable *Kṣmāṃ* is added to the navel; the syllable *Hrīḥ* is added to the heart; the syllable *A* is added to the throat.
By means of this empowerment, the body is made firm, such that no obstacles or demons whatsoever can prevail.
This is harmful. Regarding the empowerment of the four places, there are two explanations (but only the former should be used).
If a person knows that they fully understand all Buddhas of the three times, they should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm:
everything is created by mind alone.

Next, form the Seal for Breaking Hell (with both hands in vajra-fists, hooking the two wisdom fingers together, and extending the forefingers and middle fingers to support one another). Contemplate opening the hells;
recite the mantra for opening [the gates] three times with three pulls: [Mantra follows]
Namaḥ āṣṭāṣṭa-satvānāṃ samyaksaṃbuddha-koṭīnām.
Oṃ cūla-nā va-paśye tiri-tiri hūṃ. (The mantra and mudrā may be understood as before.
One should visualize oneself as the increasing red-colored Avalokiteśvara.)
She has two faces and two arms. At the three locations—the tongue, the heart center, and the seal (mudrā)—there are red syllables *hrīḥ*, all emitting light. As [described above].
The light of the rising sun shines upon and touches the hells, causing them all to be destroyed. A question is asked:
"If emitting light from a single location is sufficient to destroy them, why are three used? The answer is: "Because those hells are for sentient beings."
Because the three karmas are falsely created, one now likewise employs the emission of light through these three karmas to destroy them.

Furthermore, it was asked: "The hells are formed by the individual karma of sentient beings; how can they be destroyed? The answer is: Although they are called individual karma, they are fundamentally of one mind.
When illuminated by wisdom, even sentient beings do not exist—how then could there be hells? It is due to delusion regarding the one mind [that they appear].
Thus, one falsely creates various evils; when these evil karmas ripen, one falsely perceives the existence of hell.

Having fallen into hell, one falsely experiences suffering—just as in a dream, one may be devoured by tigers, wolves, or lions, or bound by bandits, or encounter royal calamities, undergoing all manner of sufferings.
Yet upon waking from the dream, nothing at all is found. Now, observe this hell.
Suffering is likewise thus. By employing the power of illumination, there is nothing that cannot be shattered. Question:

Since hell is fundamentally empty in this way, why is it necessary to shatter it in order to save those within? Answer: Although I, by means of wisdom, illuminate and know its fundamental emptiness, they lack such illuminating wisdom;
how then could they not suffer? Therefore, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "While dreaming, it is not non-existent," and so on.
Upon awakening, there is nothing to be found. Now, I intend precisely to shatter this hell and its suffering-emptiness.
If one traces it back to its origin, since that hell is formed through the causal conditions of evil karma, one knows it does not truly exist.

I now employ wisdom to illuminate these causal conditions and thus destroy them: first, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); second, hand-seals (*mudrā*); third, mantras; and fourth, ritual action (*kriyā*).
Contemplation. With these five kinds of causal conditions—the illumination of the five wisdoms—what task could not be accomplished? How could it be that they merely destroy the hells?
Nowadays, those who study [the Dharma] indiscriminately call themselves *ācāryas*, doing nothing more than making sounds by shaking bells and clapping cymbals;
many of them surely fear they will fail to fulfill the intentions of their patrons.

By the majestic spiritual power of this mudrā and mantra, all the gates to the hells within the various realms of existence shall open wide of their own accord upon encountering this mudrā and mantra.
We now reverently invoke the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.
(Recite the formal invitation while holding incense and flowers. When the assembly has finished chanting in unison, the leader holds the incense burner and invites:
Namo! With single-minded devotion, we respectfully invite you: You shall realize Bodhi only when all sentient beings have been delivered; you vow not to become a Buddha until the hells are emptied.
Great Holy Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, we pray that you will not violate your original vow and take pity [upon us].
Out of compassion for sentient beings, you have graced this Dharma assembly with your presence at this hour tonight.

(The assembly offers incense and flowers in unison; the Master places them in the incense burner, performs the four *cakra-mudrās*, recites *jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ*, forms the mudrā while silently reciting, extends the five offerings, and proclaims the memorial petitions for the ancestral spirits and deceased relatives.)

With single-minded devotion, I invoke the sovereign emperors of successive reigns and the feudal lords and kings of past dynasties, who dwell aloft within the nine-layered palace halls and alone command the mountains and rivers across ten thousand *li*.
(Recite: The warships that came from the West have suddenly gathered their imperial aura after a thousand years; the imperial carriage that departed for the North—
The cries of grievance from the five kingdoms have not yet ceased. (Alas! The cuckoo calls as the peach blossoms fall under the moon;

blood stains the branches, and the resentment remains ever long. May all such as the former kings and later lords, this assembly of solitary spirits, by the power of the Triple Gem and relying upon secret mantras, come now at this very hour to this Dharma assembly.
(All together accept this unobstructed nectar-food of the Dharma. With single-minded devotion, they invoke [the deities]:
erecting altars and enshrining generals, hoisting banners and enfeoffing barons. Their strength shifts the thousand-jin golden cauldron; their person serves as a ten-thousand-li long wall. (Recite:
The morning mist chills the leopard-patterned tent; in vain was the toil of horses sweating under the sun. The winds have ceased and the smoke of the wolf-sign has subsided.
In vain did they bear the hope of "climbing the dragon. (Alas! Where now are the warhorses of the generals?
Wild grasses and idle flowers fill the earth with sorrow. Such as these—the ranks of heroes and commanders, and all classes of solitary spirits—[and so forth].

With single-minded devotion, I invoke the talented and eminent of the five imperial tombs and the virtuous and worthy of the hundred commanderies—those who have served with pure integrity for three years and report their loyalty to the sovereign with a heart as crimson as cinnabar.
(Prose: From southern prefectures and northern counties, long departed from the villages of our native lands; from the edges of the sea and the ends of the earth.
Far away they have perished on the islands of Penglai. (Alas! Their official status has withered like the flowing waters;
their wandering souls are shrouded in obscurity, separated by the Yang Pass. Such are the ranks of civil officials and chief ministers—a multitude of solitary spirits, and so forth.

With single-minded devotion, I invoke the talents of the academy and the scholars of humble dwellings: those who have trodden the path through the literary groves as "Plum-Flower Seekers," and those whose bodies have wandered the halls of the imperial examination court by means of their strategic essays.
(In the interlude: The glow-worm lamp flickered out; three years of toil were in vain. The iron inkstone was worn through to the bottom.
For ten years they have endured the hardships of arrogant ambition. (Alas! Seven feet of crimson silk inscribe their names;
a mound of yellow earth covers their literary achievements. Such are the ranks of scholars and examination candidates—this entire class of solitary spirits, and so forth.

With single-minded devotion, I invoke the transcendent masters who have emerged from the mundane world, the eminent monks with flying staffs, the pure practitioners who diligently cultivate the five precepts, and the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs of holy conduct.
(Addressing them: Amidst yellow chrysanthemums and verdant bamboos, we discuss in vain the secret and sublime truths; even the white oxen and tawny slaves [are enlightened].
In vain he recited the wondrous verses on suffering and emptiness. (Alas! By the window of the sutra hall, the cold moon of the third watch is reflected;
in the meditation chamber, the empty brightness of the midnight lamp shines. Such are the ranks of the black-robed śrāmaṇeras, a class of awakened spirits and the like... (and so forth).

With single-minded devotion, I invoke those in yellow caps and rustic garb, and the immortals in feathered robes. They cultivate the truth within the Peach Blossom Spring and nurture their nature before the islands of Langyuan.
(Recitation: Through the refinement of the three flowers and nine elixirs, they have not yet been permitted to register their names in the Celestial Registry; for the four elements are impermanent.
The Underworld finds it difficult to permit the extension of one’s allotted lifespan. (Alas! At Linguan, the frost is cold and the alchemical furnaces are chill;

at the altar of the incantation, the wind is bleak and the apricot blossoms are sparse. Such are the ranks of the Daoist masters of the Mysterious Gate, along with the various classes of distant spirits and the multitude [of the assembly] (and so forth).

With single-minded devotion, I invoke you: those traveling on rivers and lakes, merchants journeying north and south, wandering ten thousand *li* in pursuit of wealth, and trading with thousands of gold pieces in accumulated goods.
(Recite: The winds and frost are unpredictable; one’s body may be smeared as oil within the belly of a fish. The roads are difficult to guard against; [may you protect us from such perils].
Their lives were lost on the perilous path of the Yangcheng Pass. (Alas! Their lingering spirits follow the clouds northward as they darken;
their souls as guests pursue the waters eastward as they flow on. Such are the multitude of solitary spirits among the ranks of travelers in a foreign land... (and so forth).
With single-minded devotion, he invokes the warriors in their armor and the stalwart soldiers on the battlefield. Amidst the shadows of red banners they vie for supremacy;

amidst the clusters of white blades they risk their lives. (Prose: As soon as the drums and gongs first resound, in an instant their bellies burst and their entrails are pierced. Victory and defeat are then distinguished.
Throughout the earth, limbs are mangled and heads are shattered. (Alas! Vast stretches of yellow sand resound with the wailing of ghosts;
boundless white bones lie where few have come to gather them. Such are the ranks of soldiers fallen in battle, this multitude of solitary spirits, and so forth.

With single-minded devotion, you invoked [the deity]; for ten months you carried him in your womb; for three days you sat upon the grass. First, you rejoiced at the harmonious cries of phoenixes and peacocks;

next, you looked forward to the auspicious dreams of bears and cubs. (Recite: As we respectfully prepare to sing the hymn, fortune and misfortune depend but on a brief moment. Before the jade vessel and the broken tile are distinguished, [we pray for your grace].

Mother and child alike return to the long night. (Alas! Like flowers in full bloom struck by a sudden rainstorm, or the moon at its brightest shrouded by dark clouds—such are the multitudes of solitary spirits, including those who have suffered the hardships of childbirth within the Blood Lake, and so forth. (etc.)
With single-minded devotion, I invoke those of the Rong, Yi, Man, and Di; the mute, the blind, and the deaf; the laborers who lose their lives for hire;

and the concubines and handmaidens whose bodies are wounded by jealousy. (I declare: Those who have slighted and deceived the Triple Gem, whose transgressions accumulate like the sands of the Ganges, and who have been rebellious toward their parents.
Villainy floats throughout the universe. (Alas! The long night stretches on interminably; when will it dawn?
At the hidden barrier of the netherworld, spring remains unknown. Such are the masses of solitary spirits—those who are stubbornly perverse and rebellious (and so forth).

With single-minded devotion, she summons the beautiful maidens of the inner palace, the exquisite ladies of the chambers, whose faces vie for beauty with rouge and powder, and whose robes compete for elegance, perfumed with dragon-agarwood and musk.
(Prose: The clouds have gathered and the rain has ceased; her soul is extinguished within the gardens of Jingu. The moon is waning and the flowers are withered.
My bowels are broken at the post station of Mawei. (Alas! The elegance of former days is nowhere to be seen;
amidst the green willows and fragrant grasses, cold skulls lie scattered. Such as we are—women with skirts and hairpins—a multitude of solitary spirits, and so forth.

With single-minded devotion, I invoke those who were hungry and cold beggars, prisoners subjected to execution, those whose bodies were wounded by water or fire, and those who lost their lives encountering tigers and wolves.
(Recite: Those who hanged themselves or took poison—their resentful spirits linger for a thousand years; those struck by lightning or buried under collapsing cliffs.
A trace of lingering terror stirs. (Alas! In the evening rain and blue smoke, cold magpies shriek; in the autumn wind and yellow leaves, crows fly in disarray.
Such are the multitudes of those who have perished by violence or unnatural death, this class of solitary spirits, and so forth.
With single-minded devotion, I invoke all those within the six realms of the dharma-realm: the ten classes of orphaned spirits, the *pīyēluó* (preta) hosts led by the Face-Afflicted (*mukhadahana*),
the myriad species that dwell upon grass and trees, the *chīmèi wǎngliǎng* (goblins and imps), the lingering souls and orphaned spirits,
and the deceased ancestors and kinsmen of myself and others— this entire assembly (and so forth).
(Paper for Transforming Lonely Spirits).
The invited spirits have all now arrived. May the Great Assembly, out of compassion, join their voices in lamentation.

As for the sovereigns of recent and former dynasties, who held positions of imperial honor; the meritorious relatives, dukes, and kings, of noble jade-lineage and golden-branch descent; and the high ministers and officials—
The ladies of the inner court—concubines, handmaidens, and queens—have severed their dreams of the Flower-Root (Huaxu) realm and come to receive the flavor of ambrosia.

The eminent men of the state and the ministers of the court, who wove the fabric of governance to assist the age and governed the common people, yet failed to fulfill the aspirations of their loyal and virtuous wills;
having lost favor and harbored sorrow, they were banished to frontier lands. With souls wandering in longing for their country, they have come to receive the flavor of ambrosia.
Generals and military officers, leading three divisions of troops, drew up battle arrays and clashed in combat; the sound of gongs and drums resounded through heaven and earth.

Fighting in the north and campaigning in the south, they perished upon the desert fields. Having sacrificed their bodies for the sake of the nation, they now come to receive the flavor of the nectar of immortality.
He studied the ancients and exhausted the Classics; a scholar whose writings were like brocade and embroidery. He reflected snow and stole light to study with bitter resolve within his cold window.
Yet fate has led him astray; his name is not upon the golden list. Now, with a heavy heart, this soul from the underworld comes to receive the flavor of the nectar of immortality.
Renouncing what is dear and bidding farewell to kin, he entered the gates of the Empty Gate early on. Seeking the Way and searching for a teacher, his sole purpose was to transcend birth and death.

As summer passed and winter came, he did not realize that impermanence had arrived; now, reflecting inwardly and turning the light back upon himself, he comes to receive the flavor of the nectar of immortality.
Clad in feathered robes and wearing yellow caps, you have long since resolved to cultivate the Way. You refine elixirs and burn cinnabar, nurturing your nature to restore the primal qi.
Through asceticism and mental toil, you hope to ascend to the rank of an immortal. Do not cling to this discarded form; come instead to receive the flavor of the nectar of immortality.

Filial sons and worthy grandsons, men of righteousness, valor, loyalty, and goodness, as well as heroic women and chaste wives—regarding death as a return home, they upheld their integrity and forgot their own bodies, leaving behind a heroic spirit for a thousand ages.
May their lingering souls now come to partake of the flavor of the sweet nectar.
The female practitioners of the Way and the nuns dwell upon the ground of golden light; like phoenixes soaring through the void, they are untainted by worldly affairs.
Yet, failing to realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they drift through the cycle of empty birth and death. May these pure spirits come now to receive the flavor of the ambrosia (*amṛta*).

Whether one studies geography and astronomy, medicine and the principles of yin and yang, divination by hexagrams and tortoise shells, physiognomy or astrology, and speaks of auspiciousness or portends misfortune—one cannot avoid the face of impermanence.
Only by abandoning the false and returning to the true can one come to partake of the flavor of ambrosia.
Sedentary shopkeepers and traveling merchants, those engaged in various enterprises, and those skilled in many arts who seek wealth and profit through trade—
having left their wells and departed from their homelands to die in foreign lands— now come in a long journey of dreams to receive the flavor of the ambrosia.
Those who have broken the law and suffered punishment, long confined in dark prisons; those who, burdened by debt, plotted for wealth, becoming like creditors and enemies;
those afflicted by malignant diseases or natural calamities, perishing from cold or hunger—may they swiftly depart from the Yellow Springs and come to receive the flavor of sweet nectar.

Injured by horses or trampled by carts; their bodies crushed by collapsing walls; struck by ghosts or hit by thunderbolts; those who commit suicide by slashing their throats or hanging from beams; burned or swept away by water and fire;
those bitten by tigers or harmed by snakes—may these solitary spirits of the nine untimely deaths come here to receive the flavor of the nectar of immortality.
Those who drank blood or ate human hair, those born and raised in lands of barbarians, those who labored to repay debts, female and male servants,
slaves, the mute, the blind, the deaf, the disabled, and the helpless— all these suffering souls come now to receive the flavor of nectar.

They were disobedient toward their parents, bringing resentment and pollution upon Heaven and Earth; they slandered the Buddha and deceived the Sangha, destroying images and burning sutras and verses.
With deeply entrenched false views, their bitter retribution was boundless. May these ten-evil, frantic spirits now come to receive the flavor of nectar.

The Great Gate of Generosity is opened. May those who are orphaned spirits, our ancestors and deceased kin, and all classes of karmic enemies—those in the eight difficulties and the three miserable realms—equally transcend their suffering and be delivered.
Relying upon the Buddha’s radiant light, come now to receive the flavor of the ambrosia.
Amitābha Buddha, having long held boundless vows, beholds those lost on the path, constantly drifting and drowning in the sea of suffering.

With hands extended in earnest compassion, you specially launch the vessel of mercy to rescue them; you universally carry all sentient beings, so that together they may attend the assembly at the Lotus Pond.
Homage to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pond Assembly (Recite three times).

By the power of the Great Compassionate Buddha, I summon all sentient beings of the hidden and visible realms, including the hungry ghosts who have suffered from hunger and thirst for kalpas; do not disobey the Buddha’s command, but descend here.

Next, form the mudrā for summoning hungry ghosts (with the left hand forming the gesture of fearlessness, the right hand held forward with the fingers slightly bent and extended to hook and summon them).
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ jvala jvālaya hehe svāhā. (The mudrā and mantra may be understood as before;
one should visualize a white syllable Hrīḥ upon the left hand mudrā.)
The letter (ṬHA) emits light, summoning that host of spirits to the site of practice.
They circumambulate the Buddha three times, pay homage to him, and depart. Upon reaching the exterior of the altar, they remain there.
Outside the altar, it is divided into four gates:
from the eastern gate to the southern gate is the assembly of hell-beings;
from the southern gate to the southwest corner is the assembly of hungry ghosts. From...
From the southwest corner to the western gate is the assembly of animals; from the western gate to the northwest corner is the assembly of humans;
from the northwest corner to the northern gate is the assembly of asuras; from the northern gate to the eastern gate is the assembly of devas.
They should be stationed in this manner. The attendant said, "Please grant them comfort."

Once they have been summoned, they all assemble like clouds; with a heart of compassion, he praises and consoles them, causing them to rejoice, and then, as they thirst and yearn for the Dharma, [the leader speaks].
Welcome, sons of the Buddhas! Because you have previously formed superior karmic connections, you now encounter this auspicious assembly. Do not give rise to sorrow or fear;
with single-minded longing for the Dharma, do not let this moment pass. Let the precepts moisten your bodies, and you shall swiftly be led away from the realms of suffering.
"You, all you sons of the Buddhas, having encountered this place of enlightenment, shall have all your sins summoned into the vajra-palm.
Next, form the mudrā for summoning sins: (with both hands in the vajra-bind, extend the ring fingers and thumbs like needles; the index and middle fingers...)
The hook is curved like a hook. The mantra for summoning sins is: Oṃ sarvapa pakaṣaṇa cūṣṭadāna vajrasattva samaya hūṃ jaḥ.
(The Master’s seal and mantra may be understood from other sources.
One should visualize the syllable white *hrīḥ* (with the two consonants joined) upon the tips of the two middle fingers, emitting light that enters [the disciple].)
The offenses emerge from within that body, like smoke and mist merging together. It is asked:
"If offenses have no substantial reality, why is it now said to be like that?"
Does the smoke and mist have a substantial reality?
Answer: Although it lacks substantial reality, it is able to fill heaven and earth and obstruct the eyes and mind, preventing one from seeing the pure realm of the Buddhas.
Now, we borrow these mists as the objective signs (*ālambana-nimitta*) to summon forth their transgressions; they truly exist [in this sense].
It is beneficial for all affairs.
All evil karmas of sin are destroyed, just as they are extinguished by the fire at the end of an eon; once that fire is extinguished, even diamond is reduced to fine dust.
Next, bind the mudrā for destroying transgressions (the eight fingers are crossed inward;
extend the *tarjanī* and *anāmikā* like needles). The mantra for destroying transgressions is: Oṃ vajrapāṇi uṣṭra sphoṭaya sarvāpadbhyaḥ.
Bhāntanani | Vramukchaye | Sarvābhaye | Gati-vyākaraṇe | Sarvasattvānām | Sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhite | Vajrasamaye | Hūṃ | Traṭa.
(The master’s seal-mantra may be understood from the source.
At the tips of the two middle fingers,
visualize the syllable *tlaḥ* on the left and the syllable *ṭha* on the right.)
And golden. The practitioner should cause their own body to grow, visualizing the body of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva as blue and green in color. At every recitation:
Recite the mantra once. Rub and shake with the two middle fingers.
Upon reaching the final repetition, clap the hands to make a sound. Visualize that mountain of sins as being like tiles, collapsing and falling over.
The previously summoned sins, which are like smoke and mist, shall disperse instantly upon this thought. Question: Sins have no substantial essence.
[The interlocutor asks: "What is meant by 'subduing' (cui) these marks? [The Master] replies: "It is precisely because they are non-existent that they are said to be subdued.
If they were determinately existent, how could they possibly be subdued? The attendant then says: "..."
Fixed karma cannot be altered; by the power of samādhi empowerment, all obstacles and difficulties from beginningless time are completely extinguished.

Next, perform the mudrā for destroying fixed karma (with the two hands in the vajra-palms gesture, bend the second joints of the middle fingers, and press the tips of the ring and little fingers with the thumbs). The mantra for purifying karma is as follows:
Oṃ vajrakarma-cūḍāmaṇaye sarvārthānaya buddhasatye namaḥ samaya hūṃ. (The mudrā and mantra may be understood accordingly. Upon the lunar disc at the heart:)

Visualize a blue syllable *hrīḥ* emitting light that illuminates all those among the assembly of pretas who have not yet had the opportunity to repent for their transgressions since the appearance of the Buddhas in the world.
Regarding this karma, one should contemplate that its intrinsic nature is pure and fundamentally free from the notion of action.
One should observe that there is no difference between those ghostly hosts, the Buddha, and one’s own mind; this is called "shattering."
This is definitive karma. This single dharma is precisely that which severs the cognitive obscurations; let those who study this know it.
The attendant said:
"The nature of sin is fundamentally empty, yet it is created by the mind; when the mind ceases, sin likewise perishes."
When sin perishes and the mind is extinguished, both are empty; this is what is called true repentance.
Next, perform the seal for the extinction of sins through repentance (with the two hands in the *vajrabandha*, the six pāramitās forming the outer crossed arms).
Advance the force. Bend the two joints.
Press the *candra* and *jñāna* fingers upon the two *tarjanīs*). Oṃ. Sarvabāhu. Candra.
SPHATTA HTAḤ VAJRAYE SVĀHĀ. (The seal and mantra may be understood accordingly.
One should visualize the syllable HRĪḤ, white in color, upon the tips of two bent fingers.)
Light was emitted and entered the body of that ghost, like the sun melting dew.
The stains of its transgressions were dissolved and melted away like ink, flowing down from the feet and seeping into the earth until it reached the adamantine foundation (*vajra-pṛthivī*). He asked:
"Previously, you already summoned, subdued, and shattered him; why do you now perform repentance? He replied: "The previous acts were all *principle-repentance* (*li-chān*)."
"Repentance. Now, one repents for these very matters. Since principle and phenomena are unimpeded (*li-shi wu-ai*), how could there be any confusion?
Furthermore, he asked: "What kind of sin is like ink? He replied: "Sin refers to black karma (*kṛṣṇa-karman*); therefore, ink is used as a symbol.
'Juice' (*zhi*) carries the meaning of flowing and pouring; thus it is said that the sin is like ink-juice."
O sons of the Buddha, having already performed repentance, the sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas are instantly eliminated in a single thought-moment.
Like fire consuming dry grass, they are utterly extinguished without remainder.
A single drop of cool water can eliminate hunger and thirst; by sprinkling it upon the gate of the crown, all are made to attain peace and happiness.
Next, form the mudrā of the Tathāgata of Wondrous Form Bestowing Nectar (alternatively called Bestowing Coolness).
For the mudrā, rotate the left wrist forward with the fingers;
forcefully snap the thumb and forefinger while reciting the Amṛtīkaraṇa-mantra:

Question: Previously, upon entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), you yourself were the Bodhisattva; why, then, do you now again dispatch Māra to transform space? Answer:
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that after the World-Honored One had preached the *Ananta-artha*, he entered samādhi and emitted light;

This manifests the Single Dharma. It is like the ritual of the world: when one who sacrifices at the ancestral temple has already fasted and purified themselves by bathing, why do they wash their hands again upon ascending the hall? It is to express reverence.

"One must not fail to apply one's mind with focused concentration. He asked again, "For what reason do you not give them food and drink, but instead give water?
He replied, "The beings in the realm of hungry ghosts are mostly scorched by the fires of their own karma; therefore, I now give them water to douse and extinguish those karmic fires.
The Buddha said, "Those ghosts have not heard the names of even broth or water for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas."
How much more so if they were to drink it? Furthermore, it is said that those ghosts do not see water even when they are on the banks of the Ganges;

even if they should see it, it turns into pus and blood. How much more so at the time of drinking, when it enters their bellies and transforms into fierce flames, burning their hearts and stomachs with heat.

Transcending the Buddha’s compassionate salvation, you must certainly cherish one another, maintaining a thought like that of parents remembering their children.

Furthermore, for your sake, I have divided these pure offerings into three parts; one portion is to be given to the aquatic creatures.

What was performed previously still distinguished between the noble and the ordinary; therefore, one first made offerings to the Triple Gem and subsequently bestowed [alms] upon the assembly of spirits.

(Recite the *Sukhāvatī-mantra* once. This perfect empowerment (*pariṇāmanā-adhiṣṭhāna*) is twofold: first, the perfection of the divine mantra; second, the perfection of the roots of virtue. Regarding the perfection of the divine mantra: the attendant should take flowers and rice and distribute them to the assembly.

Having distributed them, the teacher and disciples chant the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī* in unison, visualizing that they become seeds of light. Once the flowers and rice have been empowered, the attendant takes some from a small plate and scatters them outside.

The teacher visualizes that all spirits, ghosts, and other beings who come into contact with this light will attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss as those of the highest grade of the highest birth. The attendant pours out the pure water for the food offering, while the teacher and disciples together recite the Six-Syllable Great Illuminator (*Ṣaḍakṣarī-mahāvidyā*).)
Having completed one hundred and eight recitations of the mantra, ring the bell and chant the six verses of the Dharma-music (*dharmarati-gāthā*).
By virtue of this merit, may all sentient beings suffering in the hells see the mountains of knives and swords and the forests of blades transformed into wish-fulfilling trees;
may the masses of fire and iron balls become lotuses and jewels. May there be auspiciousness! May those in the hells be liberated!
Thus one is able to attain perfect enlightenment.
By virtue of this wholesome merit, may those sentient beings who are hungry ghosts suffering in torment find their bodies cooled from the smoke and flames burning within their mouths;
may they be spontaneously and eternally satiated by the nectar from the hand of Avalokiteśvara. Auspiciousness! May the hungry ghosts be liberated!
And may they be able to attain perfect enlightenment.
By virtue of this wholesome merit, may those sentient beings who are owners of livestock be freed from all sufferings such as slaughter, burning, boiling, and cruel torment.
May they be freed from the ignorance of being ridden and swiftly attain great wisdom. Auspiciousness! May animals be liberated!
And may they be able to attain perfect enlightenment.

By virtue of this wholesome merit, may those sentient beings who suffer in the human realm be born like Māyā from the right side [of their mothers], may they possess the six sense faculties, forever leave the eight difficulties behind, and cultivate merit and wisdom. Auspiciousness! May there be liberation in the human realm.
And may they be able to attain perfect enlightenment.
By virtue of this wholesome merit, may those sentient beings among the asuras who suffer—those who are arrogant, deranged, crude, and impetuous—be swiftly made gentle and virtuous.
May their evil minds, jealousy, malice, and combative strife be naturally subdued. Auspiciousness! May the asuras be liberated.
Thus one is able to achieve perfect enlightenment.

By virtue of this wholesome benefit, those sentient beings who experience pleasure among the gods should, through the incentive of desire for pleasure, diligently and swiftly give rise to the vast bodhicitta.
When their celestial pleasures are exhausted, they will naturally experience joy amidst sorrow and suffering. May there be auspiciousness! May there be liberation among the gods!
Thus one is able to achieve perfect enlightenment.

By virtue of this wholesome benefit, the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas of the ten directions abandon the practices of the Small Vehicle—the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination—and advance toward the Great Vehicle, practicing the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the six perfections (*pāramitā*), and the myriad deeds. May there be auspiciousness! May the liberation of the two vehicles [be attained].
Thus one is able to achieve perfect enlightenment.

By virtue of this wholesome benefit, the courageous Bodhisattva of the First Ground—adorned with a hundred blessings and having fulfilled all practices and vows—suddenly transcends the ten grounds and realizes the stage of the "One Life Remaining" (Ekajātipratibaddha). Auspicious! The Mahāyāna is swiftly realized.
May I ultimately attain perfect enlightenment.
In this verse of dedication and aspiration,
for as long as I have not yet realized bodhi in this present life, may there be no internal or external obstacles, hindrances, or adverse conditions.
May I always encounter the most wondrous and virtuous spiritual friends, And may the practices and vows I cultivate be swiftly fulfilled.
At the time of death, may my consciousness remain free from confusion regarding the Supreme Triple Gem, And may I be reborn before the Tathāgata in the Pure Land of the West.

Relying on the sun of wisdom and the light of the Dharma through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one cuts off delusions and realizes the truth; thus, out of compassion for sentient beings, [one honors] the supreme Triple Gem.

Whether one proceeds before the Buddha’s assembly in a pure land according to one's karma, or lacks the roots of goodness and is not born within that sublime gathering—[it is all determined by one's prior conduct].
May I follow the wheel of karma through every birth in successive lives, constantly cultivating roots of goodness with uninterrupted habituation.

May I be born in a central land through the supreme aspiration in the Three Jewels and diligently practice the True Dharma, remaining free from illness and long-lived, with all necessities fully provided.
With the excellence of the marks and signs, eloquence, wisdom, and so forth, Possessing these seven merits, one attains the supreme human body of the Three Jewels.
May I leave home in youth and encounter a virtuous and holy teacher; Thereupon, may I attain the three types of training and maintain them with protection.
At all times, may right mindfulness and the sublime Dharma attend me; may the wondrous and supreme Guru be pleased.
May the Three Sublime Jewels, the seven types of supreme wealth, and the most excellent spiritual friends never depart from me for even a moment, just as the sun and its light are inseparable.
May I also be free from pride, doubt, and hesitation, and possess contentment; May I abandon evil conditions that are like poisonous spirits;
In the presence of the Supreme Triple Gem, the source of merit and the foundation of my supreme vows, I pray that I may constantly take refuge and offer worship.
The three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion are like the great earth; one should never give rise to them.
One should perceive the objects of the six sense-fields, such as forms and other phenomena, through the vision of the Three Supreme Jewels, realizing them to be like a mirage or a magical illusion.
May I remain unstained by attachment to the objects and spheres of the five desires;

may I never forget the supreme Bodhicitta, the Three Jewels, and all the profound and subtle teachings of the Mahāyāna; and may I constantly practice and study with diligence, as if my head were on fire.
When you realized the peerless, ultimate Bodhi, With the four means of attraction, you could rescue those in the six realms;
As the supreme Triple Gem, you could rescue those in the five turbidities. O Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara, And King Kṣitigarbha of vast vows during the final age.
All the worthy and holy ones, the Dharma-protecting deities who bear witness, protect, and mindfully observe the Dharma; the most supreme Three Jewels who blaze with radiant power;
the various protective deities of the state, the Dharma, and the stupas and temples—may their majestic virtue and blazing splendor turn back and ward off all great boundary-obstructions.
May the venomous classes of enemies, Māras, and non-Buddhists be utterly destroyed; may the venomous classes of nāgas, ghosts, and celestial bodies be struck with terror.
May the Three Supreme Jewels swiftly cause the three calamities and five turbidities to be eliminated; may the seven hardships and eight fears be extinguished in a single thought-moment.
The hundred grains are abundant and all things flourish; the seven treasures are sufficient and the five flavors are fully provided.
With the supreme Triple Gem, one receives and enjoys the four requisites for offerings without lack; by cultivating the eight fields of merit, one attains auspiciousness and peace.
Throughout the land, may the Buddha’s activities flourish and the Wheel of Dharma turn; may the merit and wisdom of sentient beings increase and all be brought to perfection.
Through the power of the supreme Three Jewels, the causal conditions of our own roots of virtue, and the power of the blessings of the Guru, Yidam, and Dakini.
By the majestic power of the secret mantras of the true dharma of the Triple Gem, may whatever vows are made be swiftly fulfilled.
Through the supreme Triple Gem,
which is capable of bestowing back upon the giver what has been given, and through the goodness of that returning gift, may all the various merits thus obtained be [dedicated].
Like an illusion, an illusion resembles a dream; The three spheres are empty of intrinsic nature, and that emptiness is utterly pure.
This is the auspicious verse of the supreme Three Jewels.
May there be auspiciousness by day and auspiciousness by night; may the Guru compassionately take me into his care.
May there be constant auspiciousness throughout the six periods of day and night; may the Three Jewels compassionately take me into their care.
May all things be auspicious at all times; may the Dharma protectors always provide protection.
Homage to the Tathāgata Amitāyus of the Western Quarter and to the ocean-like assembly of great Bodhisattvas and holy multitudes.

We pray that the transgressions of all beings within the Dharma-realm, both living and deceased, may be eliminated; that they may be reborn together in the Pure Land, and that we may dedicate these merits toward unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi.

I humbly submit this preface:

Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored, the cataracts of the sense organs are removed and the dust is extinguished, so that awareness becomes perfectly pure.
For the true source is profoundly tranquil; thus, the nature of sin is fundamentally empty. The ocean of suffering is vast and deep, following the waves of delusion.
It does not cease; moved by the karma of sentient beings, they remain submerged for long kalpas, receiving retribution within the hells where they suffer eternal torment.
Reborn among the hungry ghosts, they endure hunger and emptiness for a long time. Since there is no prospect of liberation, how could there be a path to transcendence?
Were it not for the compassionate vows of the Tathāgata, how could the inverted suspension of the evil realms be resolved?
Chanting the mantras as the ultimate exposition, I bestow the Dharma-food of ambrosia; lighting the precious torches of lamps, I illuminate the dark paths of the obscured realms.

May all wandering beings in delusion together transcend to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Today, at this site of practice, I dedicate these merits universally to the Great Being Face-Afflicted (Yamen Dashi), who governs the thirty-six divisions of spirits within the Iron Ring Mountains—an infinite and boundless number, like the sands of the Ganges.

For the multitude of hungry ghosts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges: we pray that from vast eons past until this present life, their karmic obstructions may be dissolved and melted away, and their transgressions may be washed clean and purified.
May the boiling cauldrons of molten bronze transform into lotus ponds endowed with the eight virtues;
may the interlacing flames of the furnaces become fragrant canopies of the seven treasures; and may the sword-trees all become jade trees, and the mountain of blades entirely transformed.
The mountain of jewels; the iron beds pervading the world manifest as the Dharma-throne of Bodhi; the cauldrons filled with molten copper are transformed into the supreme nectar of *amṛta*.
Meeting here with creditors from former lives, all are granted liberation; encountering enemies from kalpas past, they gather together.

Each attained a state of carefree wandering; the jailers gave rise to compassion, and the infernal officials upheld virtue. From this point on, the parents of many lifetimes entered the ranks of the sages and transcended the mundane;

from this time forth, kinsmen and relatives of successive generations received grace and obtained blessings. The five signs of decline no longer appeared in the heavens, and the four marks were all seen as empty in the human realm.
The asuras abandoned all hearts of anger, and the various sufferings and afflictions in hell ceased. As for the *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* number of hungry ghosts—
May the heat of affliction be transformed into coolness; may the ten classes of sentient beings abandon the path of delusion and ascend to the shore of enlightenment.
May it be universally prayed that in this land, other lands, and immeasurable lands, all sentient beings together realize the true and eternal.
May in this world, other worlds, and immeasurable worlds, all inexhaustible conscious beings equally attain the Buddha-way. [To repay] the four debts of gratitude...
